title: Open the first crates, trust the rest
allegory: Upfront auditing is like a dock inspector who may open only two crates in every hundred and opens the first ones to arrive, then waves every later crate through, so a smuggler who smuggles only rarely will usually get the first contraband past after the inspections are over.
map: the brilliant supplier you cannot fully trust
U: the untrusted, more capable model writing the solutions
an inspector who may open only 2 crates in every 100
H: the human audit budget, 2% of submissions
opening the first crates to arrive, then waving the rest through
upfront auditing: audit the first N submissions, accept the rest unchecked
a smuggler who smuggles rarely, betting the first one arrives after the checks
the red team's best response: backdoor only a small fraction of problems
getting through the whole season without one smuggled crate
safety: P(no backdoor submitted across the entire run)

cap.1: You have a brilliant programmer you cannot fully trust, and time to personally check only 2 of every 100 solutions. How do you spend those checks?
cap.2: AI control assumes the capable model might be trying to sabotage you. Greenblatt et al. gave the blue team a weaker trusted model and a 2% human audit budget.
cap.3: Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger (Redwood Research, ICML 2024): untrusted U, trusted weaker T, human audits on 2% of APPS submissions, and a red team hiding backdoors.

cap.1: An inspector may open 2 crates in 100. Upfront auditing opens the very first ones, then waves the rest through. A patient smuggler just bides their time.
cap.2: Upfront auditing: humans audit the first 2% of U's submissions and everything after is accepted unchecked. It needs no trusted model at all.
cap.3: The weakness is timing, not the auditor: the budget is spent before most attacks happen. Safety counts only a run with zero backdoors submitted.

cap.1: Strike often and the first strike lands inside the audit: caught. Strike rarely and it usually lands after. The attacker's sweet spot is rare.
cap.2: A toy run: 1000 problems, the first 20 audited, a caught attempt ends the run. Safety dips to about 10% at a strike rate near 0.4%. The paper's setting gave 15%.
cap.3: Safety(r) = 1 − (1−r)^k + (1−r)^n: first attempt inside the k audits, or no attempt at all. Minimised near r ≈ ln(n/k)/(n − k); the red team picks r knowing the protocol.

cap.1: The whole protocol is one question per solution: is it among the first few? Yes: a human checks it. No: it goes straight out, unread.
cap.2: Audit the first N submissions, where N is the audit budget times the run length, and submit U's code unchanged for the rest. No trusted model is involved.
cap.3: The rule looks only at a submission's position, never its content, so a red team that attacks rarely is seldom inside the audited window. Content-aware protocols spend the same budget better.

chapters.verdict: Safety is a worst case: score the protocol against the attacker's best response.

cap.1: Test against an attacker who strikes every time and the very first strike is caught. The protocol looks perfect. A patient attacker is the real test.
cap.2: Safety is a worst case over red-team strategies, and the red team knows the protocol. Always score a protocol against the attacker's best response, not your first guess.
cap.3: Safety is P[no backdoor submitted] under the red team's best response to the protocol. A fixed, weaker attack policy overstates it; ARENA's Pareto section lists this caveat.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The floor every protocol must beat
Spend checks by risk, not by the clock

cap.1: Upfront auditing is the simplest safety plan and the floor to beat. Spending the same checks where things look riskiest does far better.
cap.2: Same 2% budget: upfront auditing 15% safe at 100% usefulness, trusted monitoring 62%, defer-to-trusted 83%, trusted editing 92% at 94% usefulness.
cap.3: For steering AI: control asks what you can guarantee from a model that may be scheming. Where the budget went, not detector quality alone, moved safety from 15% to 62%.

params.label: audit budget, spent upfront (% of the run)

readouts.label: submissions audited

caption.1: Drag the strike rate. Strike often and you are caught in the first audits. Strike rarely and the first strike lands after them. Then raise the budget.
caption.2: A toy, not the paper: every strike is a working backdoor and a caught one ends the run. At 2% the attacker's best rate leaves about 10% safety; the paper reports 15%.
caption.3: Safety(r) = 1 − (1−r)^k + (1−r)^n, minimised where (1−r)^(n−k) = k/n. The worst case depends mainly on the budget fraction: 20% upfront still leaves under half.

where_else: Any spot-check schedule an adversary can predict: the gaps between fixed checks are where a patient attacker waits
Code review that only reads a project's first changes leaves every later change unexamined
Risk-based auditing in finance and security, which spends a fixed checking budget where things look riskiest

hamming.what: The simplest AI control protocol: humans audit the first slice of an untrusted model's submissions, up to the audit budget, and accept everything after that unchecked.
hamming.when: As the baseline in a control evaluation: the floor that monitoring, deferral and editing protocols must beat, measured on safety and usefulness together.
hamming.why: It shows why timing matters: an attacker who strikes rarely usually strikes after the budget is spent, so the same checks do far more when steered by suspicion.

object.title: The safety valley
object.subtitle: A toy control run as a landscape: across, how often the attacker strikes; along, how big the upfront audit budget is; height, the chance nothing bad gets through.

marks.label: attacker's sweet spot at a 2% budget

cap.1: Safety as a landscape: one way, how often the attacker strikes; the other, how big your upfront budget is. Height is the chance nothing gets through.
cap.2: Toy model: 1000 problems, a caught attempt ends the run. Every point is one attacker strategy against one budget.
cap.3: S(r, a) = 1 − (1−r)^(an) + (1−r)^n. The blue team fixes the budget; the red team then picks r at the bottom of the valley.

cap.1: There is a deep valley at rare strikes. That valley is where a smart attacker lives.
cap.2: At a 2% budget the valley bottoms out near a 0.4% strike rate with about 10% safety, the same ballpark as the paper's 15%.
cap.3: The minimum sits near r ≈ ln(n/k)/(n − k): rare enough to miss the k audits, frequent enough to strike once in the remaining n − k.

cap.1: More budget lifts the valley floor, but slowly. Even auditing the first 20% leaves safety under half.
cap.2: Upfront spending buys little, because the attacker simply strikes less often.
cap.3: Worst-case safety is 1 − a^(a/(1−a)) + a^(1/(1−a)) for budget fraction a, whatever the run length: about 0.10 at 2%, 0.47 at 20%.

cap.1: From above, the valley bends: the bigger your budget, the rarer the attacker's best strike rate.
cap.2: At a 2% budget the sweet spot is about 0.4%; at 20%, about 0.2%.
cap.3: r* ≈ ln(1/a) / (n(1 − a)) shrinks as a grows, so a bigger upfront budget just pushes the attacker to strike more rarely.

cap.1: At the edges you are safe: strike too often and you are caught at once; never strike and nothing bad happens.
cap.2: An eager attacker is caught by the first audit, which is why testing only against eager attackers makes this protocol look great.
cap.3: Report safety against the red team's best response to the protocol; a weaker fixed attack policy overstates it.

predict.q: Your test attacker plants a backdoor in every solution. Under upfront auditing, what safety do you measure?

options.t: Near 100%: the very first one is audited and caught

predict.why: An eager attacker is caught in the first audit. The worst case is a patient one, which is why safety is measured against the attacker's best response.

predict.q: Upfront auditing scores 100% usefulness in the paper. Why?

options.t: It never replaces or edits U's code, so every correct solution goes through
The audits fix any wrong answers

predict.why: Usefulness is measured with an honest U. Upfront auditing changes nothing it submits, so its whole cost is on the safety side: 15%.

predict.q: Spend the same 2% budget on the submissions a trusted model rates most suspicious. What happened to safety in the paper?
predict.why: Trusted monitoring spreads the budget across the run by suspicion. Even a detector catching about a third of backdoors turns the same checks into far more safety.

object.where: Any fixed-schedule check an adversary can predict, from inspections to code review: the gaps between checks are where a patient attacker waits.
